searches.note: Twenty three searches of a share of twenty eight, five left unspent, none of them the author's. Seven were restricted to a house's own domain (arlay.com with domaine-arlay.com twice, domainedupelican.fr twice) or to the Jura wine council and the INAO (jura-vins.com and inao.gouv.fr three times: the serving advice, the years of the four decrees, the soils of Château-Chalon), and are read as primary through their summaries; the other sixteen went to the open web for the second source of a date, a person or a place. The search for the years of the decrees served three records and is counted once, under Tissot. One search, on the adoption at Pupillin, returned nothing on the house and is counted. No WebFetch was tried. Every record was tested; no fact that rests on no source was kept.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the Jura wine council's and the INAO's texts for the appellation rules the records lean on (Château-Chalon, vin de paille, the years of the decrees), then to the houses' own pages for their own dates and methods (Arlay, Pélican), then to the open web for the second source of each date, person and place.

Where two pages of one house disagree (Arlay's 1269 and 1266, its three and four years in cask) the record gives the span or both as the house's account; where the sources disagree on a year (Macle's son, Overnoy's handover) the record gives no year.

Sources whose title or address names a living person (the Wine Scholar Guild's and Raisin's Overnoy entries, the Tissot merchants whose addresses carry the son's name, the domaine's own Tissot address) were read in the results but never cited here; the fragment's own sources were left as the author wrote them.

tested: The four years without Château-Chalon (1974, 1980, 1984, 2001): The Oxford Companion to Wine on ckbk and a Swiss merchant's account both give them; neither says the wine went unmade, so the story, the card and the key now say no wine was released under the name.
The appellation of 1936, its four communes (Château-Chalon, Domblans, Ménétru-le-Vignoble, Nevy-sur-Seille) and Savagnin alone: the cahier and the INAO's page, through search: confirmed.

Sixty months under the veil and held until December of the sixth year: a sommelier school's summary of the cahier (until 15 December of the sixth year, at least sixty months under the veil, released from 1 January of the seventh) and the INAO's more than six years: kept, with the clause left open for the integrator.
The grey and blue marl slopes: the cahier (grey marls of the Lower Jurassic below a limestone cliff, slopes up to 45 per cent) and the INAO's page (scree over the blue marls): confirmed.

The family since 1850: Gault et Millau, the Wine Scholar Guild and two merchants: confirmed. The domaine as the father built it in the 1960s (1964 by Hachette, 1966 by another guide) and its reputation his (the Wine Scholar Guild): confirmed, with the mayoralty cut and the son's year cut.
Serving at 14 to 16 degrees, opened hours ahead or decanted, with Comté: the Jura wine council's guide and its recipe sheets: confirmed.
The cellars: in the heart of the village and of the sixteenth century in the results, not beneath the village: reworded.
The house rules: nobody living named (the son, his wife and his sister described or left out), no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash.

The history: the estate's history page and its visit page through search (1269 on the one and 1266 to 1315 on the other for the first lord of the Chalon-Arlay line, the countess's purchase of about 1770, her death in 1794, her Arenberg grandson in 1825, the Laguiche father and son from 1960): confirmed save the year, now the 1260s.

The salt: Wikipedia's history of Jura salt (Salins bought by the house of Chalon in 1237) and a heritage synthesis (the family's prosperity on the salt of Salins, a fortress at Arlay): the fortune now the house of Chalon's.

The vin de paille: Poulsard, Trousseau, Chardonnay and Savagnin, three to four months on racks, more than three kilograms to a half bottle, the grapes ripe and free of rot: the estate's product page and its older wine page: confirmed; the ageing four years on one page and three on the other: now three or four.

The rules of vin de paille: at least six weeks of drying (the Jura tourist board, with the author's cahier) and the four grapes (the INAO's opposition text for Arbois): confirmed. The Côtes du Jura of 1937: the Jura wine council's pages: confirmed.
The oldest château vineyard in France: the estate's own two pages, hedged as what it calls itself: kept.
The house rules: the Laguiche father, son and grandson never named; the countess and the Arenberg grandson described; no hectares.
